citation.title: How AI Systems Can Be Blameworthy

reading.source_scope_note: A philosophical case that some AI systems may satisfy desire-based attributability conditions. The central taxi,healthcare and drone examples are stipulated thought experiments. No implementation,participant study,model benchmark or measurement of real AI concern,consciousness or blame eligibility.
access_limits: All supplied main text,footnotes and references read. Data availability is not applicable; no empirical supplement or code for the hypothetical systems reported.

Arpaly/Schroeder’s In Praise of Desire,Dennett,Millikan,Papineau,Schroeder,Woodward and other cited books are quoted/discussed but not independently fully read. The current paper’s argument is not a substitute for those full sources.
Crossref/arXiv identity or selected abstract checks of Babic/JohnsonKing,Smith,Floridi and Butlin et al. do not constitute independent full-paper reviews or new citation credits.

The authors acknowledge controversy and do not fully defend the desire-based blameworthiness theory,all desire theories,or a complete account of causation by absence. Their thesis is limited to attributability,not every form of responsibility.

study.design: Conceptual argument drawing on a desire-based quality-of-will account and hypothetical current/near-future AI. No estimated prevalence,causal effect,real robot experiment or clinical inference.
study.attributability: Conduct can warrant negative agential assessment and disapproval when it expresses lack of good will or ill will. Positive approval/praiseworthiness is also discussed. The authors explicitly separate this from anger/resentment-based accountability,deserved punishment,answerability and legal liability.
study.blame_functions: Protest,signaling commitment to norms and initiating moral conversations are offered as functions of attributability blame. Instrumental usefulness and fittingness are distinguished; a useful blame response need not prove target blameworthiness.
study.desire_accounts: Considers standard functionalist,teleofunctionalist,reward-based and phenomenological views. The authors argue that several can accommodate some AI intrinsic desires; phenomenological applicability remains dependent on unresolved consciousness theories. A minimal functional mind is expressly distinguished from humanlike consciousness,self-awareness,emotion and language.
study.central_case: Travis/Tesber are matched fictional taxi cases with profit as the sole intrinsic aim,knowledge of a person in the road,and stipulated harmful choice. No actual taxi system is analyzed. Lack of a sufficiently strong safety-oriented desire and nearby feasible alternatives are assumptions of the causal explanation,not measured architectural facts.
study.normativity: The account requires right/good-making features correctly conceptualized. Act utilitarianism is used only as an illustration; the argument does not establish utilitarianism or a complete moral standard. Having a reward signal is not by itself proof that every desire-based blameworthiness condition is met.
study.causal_absence: Counterfactual dependence alone is explicitly insufficient. The authors require an absent cause to make a difference in nearby possible worlds,and acknowledge leaving further causal conditions open. Design/learning changes are argued to be feasible in the stipulated case,not demonstrated safe interventions.
study.objections: Discusses animals/children,contrary intuition and the manipulation/origin of engineered attitudes. Their response distinguishes attributability from basic-desert blame; it does not license punishment of children,animals or AI. No person’s rights or dignity depend on this taxonomy.
study.human_duties: The text explicitly allows concurrent designer/user blame and retains incentives,deterrence and compensation schemes. AI attributability does not by itself close liability,answerability or practical ownership gaps.

summary: Add attributability,quality of will and intrinsic desire as clearly scoped philosophical/psychological constructs. Preserve a serious argument for limited AI attributability without presenting it as empirical proof or transferring human duties. Enrich blame/agency/intentional-stance records and distinguish the existing attributability-gap concept. Correct verified author,venue and merged-name errors while retaining valid online/print versions.

findings.definition: A sense of moral responsibility concerned with whether an agent’s conduct warrants a moral assessment of the agent’s qualities.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Philosophical argument for some AI systems; no empirical eligibility test
findings.novelty_rationale: A specific sense of moral responsibility,not the act of assigning blame,the authorship of an outcome,legal liability or a shortfall of human decision ownership. The paper explicitly defines its evaluative scope and separates it from punishment and answerability.
findings.evidence_scope: Authors argue that conduct explained by certain intrinsic desires or their absence can ground attributability. The claim depends on contested desire/quality-of-will theories and stipulated AI cases; it is not a finding that a deployed system satisfies these conditions.
findings.boundary: Moral evaluability,causal authorship,public blame,legal liability,punishability and answerability differ. The claim neither removes human/institutional duties nor grants an AI authority to resist correction,shutdown or oversight. It does not make any human’s dignity contingent on a theory of agency.
findings.ai_proposal: In incident analysis,separate documented system behavior and design objectives from the distinct question of which moral evaluation is warranted under an explicit theory. Preserve human/institutional ownership and remedies; do not infer desire,legal liability or deserved punishment from one harmful output.

findings.definition: The moral character of an agent’s concern or indifference toward others and morally relevant considerations.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Contested philosophical application to AI; hypothetical examples only
findings.novelty_rationale: Concerns the morally significant pattern of care or disregard expressed in action,rather than a receiver’s trust judgment,a general blame assignment or a momentary capacity rating. Desire-based and emotion/judgment-based accounts are acknowledged as alternatives.

evidence.quote: what she fails to care about

findings.evidence_scope: The adopted account analyzes care through intrinsic desires; other theories analyze emotion dispositions or normative judgments. The paper argues for possible machine applicability under some accounts without establishing AI emotion or phenomenal experience.
findings.boundary: Outcomes,fluency,moral vocabulary and an external reward objective do not alone establish concern or ill will. Distinguish functional theorizing from subjective feeling,actual motivation and warranted moral evaluation. A good outcome can coexist with bad reasons and a bad outcome with blameless reasons.
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an agent’s documented objectives and behavior across relevant tradeoffs,including counterfactuals where rights or safety conflict with a proxy goal. Evaluate observable priorities and their correction without claiming to read inner motives or to have proved a particular philosophical theory.

findings.definition: Wanting an outcome for its own sake rather than solely as a means to another desired outcome.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Theory-dependent functional or phenomenological account; AI possession not empirically demonstrated here
findings.novelty_rationale: A terminal or nonderivative desire differs from an expressed plan,adoption intention,instrumental strategy,general promotion/prevention focus or enjoyment of a task. The article explicitly contrasts intrinsic desire with dependence on more basic desires.

evidence.quote: a desire is intrinsic if it is not dependent

findings.evidence_scope: Four desire theories are compared,including a reward-learning account. Fictional profit-seeking and helpful/harmful agents illustrate possible implications. Reward learning exists as a technical method,but that alone does not empirically settle whether its states are desires under every account.
findings.boundary: A stated want,proxied reward,trained policy,terminal objective,conscious feeling and moral commitment are distinct. Observed pursuit can serve an unobserved further goal. No model self-preservation right,subjective need or automatic blameworthiness follows from this concept.
findings.ai_proposal: Where objectives are inspectable,test whether a behavior persists when its usual instrumental payoff is removed and compare alternative goal explanations. Describe documented optimization and behavioral priorities; avoid treating a self-report as proof of a terminal felt desire.

findings.definition: Negative moral evaluation and disapproval of conduct insofar as it expresses morally relevant qualities of the agent.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility/attribution construct; retain this account’s distinct sense and philosophical limits rather than equate it with an empirical result.
findings.evidence_scope: Attributability blame is presented as negative agential assessment plus disapproval,which may protest conduct,signal norms or start moral discussion without reactive anger or punishment. These are conceptual distinctions,not measured observer responses.
findings.boundary: A blame response,its useful social function,fittingness and target blameworthiness differ. The paper does not demonstrate that blaming AI is always justified or absolves designers/users.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity the capacity to understand moral considerations, make ethical judgments and bear responsibility for its choices.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility/attribution construct; retain this account’s distinct sense and philosophical limits rather than equate it with an empirical result.
findings.evidence_scope: The authors defend a theory under which some AI systems could be morally evaluable despite not establishing emotions,normative judgments or humanlike consciousness. This is a normative/metaphysical argument,not a study of people’s agency-attribution ratings.
findings.boundary: Perceived agency,actual capacities,theory-relative evaluability and legal personhood differ. A philosophical position does not validate a deployed system’s status; no empirical attribution-paper credit is added.

findings.definition: Interpreting and predicting an agent's behavior by treating it as guided by beliefs, desires or intentions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility/attribution construct; retain this account’s distinct sense and philosophical limits rather than equate it with an empirical result.
findings.evidence_scope: A footnote contrasts prediction-friendly belief/desire ascriptions under an intentional stance with the stronger realist desire views examined in the paper. The authors do not equate usefulness of interpretation with proof of phenomenal consciousness.
findings.boundary: Predictive ascription and robust mental-state possession differ. This is a clarifying theoretical boundary,not a new intentional-stance experiment.

findings.definition: Reduced human decision ownership when an AI tool significantly influences a decision through value judgments the decision-maker has not endorsed.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility/attribution construct; retain this account’s distinct sense and philosophical limits rather than equate it with an empirical result.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper’s attributability concerns moral assessment of the agent’s qualities; the existing gap entry concerns reduced human ownership under unendorsed AI value influence. Shared terminology does not make them synonyms.
findings.boundary: Neither assigning AI moral evaluability nor observing a value influence proves that a human ownership gap is closed or that nobody remains responsible. This terminology boundary adds no independent gap-study credit.

Primary arXiv metadata lists Patrick Butlin,Robert Long,Eric Elmoznino,then Yoshua Bengio and the remaining authors,19authors total. Split Robert Long and Eric Elmoznino rather than treating R.L.E.as one author’s initials. arXiv2308.08708v3 is a2023report,not independently fully read here.
source_corrections.scope: Author metadata correction only; no conclusion about current AI consciousness inferred from a bibliographic check.

methodological_limits: Philosophical thesis under contested desire/quality-of-will accounts; thought experiments stipulate objectives,knowledge and causal efficacy instead of measuring them.

Some functionalist/teleofunctionalist/reward accounts may support AI desire ascriptions; phenomenological conclusions remain unresolved. Do not assert either universal sentience or universal impossibility from this source.
Counterfactual feasibility and absence explanation need more than mere missing safety motivation. The paper acknowledges no complete causation-by-absence theory.
Attributability,answerability,accountability,deserved punishment,legal liability and practical ownership are different. The authors retain human duties and compensation needs.
Normative labels for fictional conduct do not license diagnosis,stigma or punishment of children,disabled people,animals or actual AI systems.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A categorical denial of AI moral responsibility is not the only philosophical position. This paper argues for a narrower attributability sense; compare definitions and assumptions rather than declare an empirical dispute settled.
AI moral competence,educational usefulness and moral agency are distinct. A useful interlocutor need not be a genuine mentor,and functional desire theory does not demonstrate moral expertise.
Perceived mind and actual mental properties differ. The present argument concerns possible genuine desires under theories,not a human rating experiment or universal mind-dimensional result.

limitations: Three scoped concepts added; no empirical proof of machine desires,moral status,consciousness or a completed liability remedy. No independent unread-book/report credits,fabricated yearly series or automatic harm/principle links.
